body:
Short answer: Corporate event production is the planning, equipment and crew that make a meeting, conference or company event work on stage and on screen: staging, screens, sound, lighting, streaming, show calling, network and the technicians who run it all. In New York, the AV team also manages the venue side: union rules, freight elevator windows, insurance certificates and tight load-in times. Here is what the team handles, from first call to strike.

[[IMAGE]]

This guide covers what corporate event AV includes, who is on the crew, the planning timeline, run-of-show and rehearsals, presentation management, hybrid streaming, NYC venue rules, budget factors and a checklist you can use.

What corporate event production includes

Most corporate events draw from the same building blocks. A town hall needs a few; a two-day conference with breakouts needs all of them.

  • Stage — modular stage decks, stairs, skirting, a lectern, and sometimes truss for lighting and signage. Typical general-session stages run from 8x16 ft to 16x32 ft or more.
  • Screens — projection screens with laser projectors, large displays for side screens and breakouts, and confidence monitors for presenters. LED walls are rented through our sister site ledwall.nyc.
  • Sound — a PA sized to the audience, wireless lavalier and handheld mics, a mixing console, playback for walk-on music and video, and audience mics for Q&A.
  • Lighting — key and fill light so presenters look right on camera and in the back row, plus wash and color for the set and the audience.
  • Video and streaming — cameras, a switcher, image magnification (IMAG) to the screens, recording, and a stream to remote attendees.
  • Show calling — one person running the script and cueing every department.
  • Network — dedicated Wi-Fi or wired internet for streaming, presenter laptops, registration and apps, kept separate from guest Wi-Fi.
  • Crew — the technicians, operators and stagehands who install, run and strike the show.

If you want one team to own the whole technical side, that is what corporate event production in NYC looks like with us: one plan, one point of contact and one crew.

Who is on a corporate event AV crew

Crew size scales with the program. On a small meeting one technician may cover several roles.

  • Producer or technical director — owns the technical plan, the budget, the schedule and the venue coordination. Your main contact from discovery through strike.
  • A1 (audio engineer) — mixes the show, manages mics and playback, and sends a clean audio feed to the stream and recording. An A2 helps with mic swaps backstage.
  • V1 (video engineer) — runs the switcher, screens, cameras and graphics.
  • L1 (lighting designer or operator) — programs and runs the lighting desk.
  • Show caller — calls cues from the run-of-show over headset and keeps the program on time.
  • Stagehands — load in, build, and strike. At union venues, the house crew may fill some of these roles.

The timeline: from first call to strike

  1. Discovery — audience size, agenda, venue, speakers, content, remote audience and the feel you want.
  2. Site visit — the technical director checks ceiling height, rigging points, power, sight lines, the loading dock, the freight elevator and internet.
  3. Plan and quote — a stage and screen layout, equipment list, crew plan and schedule, revised until it fits the goals and budget.
  4. Pre-production — collecting slides and videos, building graphics, writing the run-of-show and confirming venue paperwork.
  5. Load-in — install, power, focus lights, test audio and video, and check the stream.
  6. Rehearsals — a tech check followed by a cue-to-cue with presenters.
  7. Show day — doors, program, breaks and any changes, all called from the run-of-show.
  8. Strike — break down and load out inside the venue's window, then deliver recordings.

Run-of-show and cue-to-cue

The run-of-show is the minute-by-minute script of the event: who walks on, which mic they wear, which slides or video play, what the lights do and how long each segment runs. It is the single document the whole crew works from, so every change should go through it.

A cue-to-cue rehearsal walks through the transitions rather than the full speeches. The crew jumps from cue to cue to confirm walk-on music, mic handoffs, video roll-ins, lighting changes and stream graphics. Plan at least an hour, more for a multi-speaker program.

Presentation and slide management

Most show-day stress comes from slides. A good conference AV setup takes them out of the presenter's hands.

  • One show machine — all decks loaded on a playback computer at the tech table, in 16:9 unless the screens say otherwise.
  • Backup laptop — a second machine mirrored and ready to take over with one switch.
  • Confidence monitors — downstage displays showing the current slide, the next slide, notes and a countdown timer.
  • Clickers — presenter remotes that talk to the show machine, with a spare at the lectern.
  • Content deadline — set a cutoff (often 48 hours before the show) and a speaker ready room on site for last-minute edits.

Hybrid events and streaming

If remote attendees are watching, treat them as a second audience. That means two or more cameras, a dedicated audio mix for the stream, a hardwired internet line, lower-thirds and a producer watching the online experience. Our hybrid event AV and streaming guide walks through platforms, bandwidth and crew in detail.

NYC venue specifics

New York adds logistics a local AV company should handle for you.

  • Union venues — many convention centers, theaters and some hotels work under labor agreements that require house stagehands for certain tasks such as rigging, power or load-in. Your crew plan has to fit those rules.
  • Freight elevator windows — office towers and many venues book the freight elevator and loading dock in fixed slots, often early morning or overnight. Missing the slot can push your load-in by hours.
  • COI — venues and building management usually require a certificate of insurance with specific additional-insured wording before they schedule load-in.
  • Load-in times — space is often booked tight around your event, so overnight or same-day load-ins are common. The schedule decides crew size.
  • Hotel ballroom in-house AV rules — hotels often have an in-house AV provider and may charge outside vendors for power, rigging or internet. Read the contract and ask about these fees before you sign.

What drives the budget

The spread between events is wide, but the same factors drive every corporate event AV quote:

  • Audience size and space — bigger audiences need bigger screens, more speakers and more light.
  • Number of rooms and breakouts — each breakout adds equipment and at least one technician.
  • Days on site — load-in, rehearsal and show days all count.
  • Labor rules and hours — union requirements, overnight work and overtime.
  • Streaming and recording — cameras, a switcher, an operator and a reliable network.
  • Staging and set — deck size, scenic elements and custom builds; see our stage rental in NYC options.

For how to read a quote, see how much event AV costs in NYC.

How to plan a corporate event: an AV checklist

  • Six to ten weeks out — confirm venue, date, audience size and agenda; book the AV team; get the venue's AV rules and COI requirements.
  • Four to six weeks out — site visit, approve the stage and screen plan, decide on streaming and recording.
  • Two to three weeks out — confirm speakers, mic needs and walk-on music; draft the run-of-show; book the freight elevator and dock.
  • One week out — final run-of-show, final crew schedule, internet confirmed, COI approved.
  • 48 hours out — all slides and videos delivered and checked on the show machine.
  • Show day — cue-to-cue complete, backup laptop tested, spare batteries on hand, stream test passed before doors.
